blocks.text: Benzene, C6H6, is one of the most important organic compounds and the simplest aromatic hydrocarbon. Many compounds derived from benzene have pleasant smells, so in the early 19th century compounds containing benzene rings were called aromatic (sweet-smelling); vanilla is an example. Hydrocarbons containing one or more benzene rings are called arenes. Today the word aromatic is used for molecules with benzene or benzene-like rings, whatever their smell; some smell unpleasant.

blocks.title: Did you know?
blocks.text: Not every good-smelling compound is aromatic. Camphor, from the camphor laurel tree, has a strong minty smell but no benzene ring in its structure.

Once the molecular formula C6H6 was known, chemists proposed several linear structures, but these could not explain benzene's properties. In 1865 the German professor August Kekule proposed a six-membered ring with alternating single and double bonds. This explained many properties, but not all of its physical and chemical behaviour.

blocks.alt: Kekule structure of benzene: a six-membered ring of C atoms, each joined to one H, with alternating single and double bonds between the carbons; beside it the same ring drawn as a skeletal hexagon with three inner double-bond lines.
blocks.caption: Kekule structure of benzene (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 60).

blocks.text: X-ray studies show that benzene is planar: a regular hexagon of six sp2-hybridised carbon atoms. Each carbon atom is joined to three other atoms, with bond angles of 120 degrees for C-C-C and H-C-C. The C-H bond is 109 pm long and the C-C bond 139 pm, between the single bond of sp3-hybridised carbons (154 pm) and the double bond of sp2-hybridised carbons (133 pm). The C-C and C-H bond lengths are 1.397 angstrom and 1.09 angstrom respectively.

blocks.alt: Benzene ring with an H on each of the six carbons. A curved arrow from the label 1.39 angstrom points to a C-C bond of the ring, and a curved arrow at one carbon marks the 120 degree angle between a ring bond and the C-H bond.
blocks.caption: Bond angles and bond lengths in benzene (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 60).
